title: Some, any, much, many, few, little
wm: Indefinite Pronouns and Adjectives of Quantity
intro: Use “some” in positive sentences and offers, “any” in negatives and most questions. “Many” and “few” go with things you can count; “much” and “little” with things you can’t. “A few” and “a little” mean “some”; “few” and “little” without “a” mean “almost none”.

rules.rule: some: positive and offers. any: negative and questions.
examples: I have some time. / I don’t have any time.
Would you like some water? Do you have any questions?

rules.rule: many / few + countable; much / little + uncountable.
“a lot of” works with both, and sounds natural in positive sentences.
examples: She has a lot of friends.
We have a lot of work.

rules.rule: a few / a little = some. few / little = not enough.
examples: I have a few friends here. (good)

mistakes.right: I have a lot of work today.
mistakes.why: In positive sentences, “a lot of” sounds more natural.

ex.q: Can I have ___ milk in my tea?
I’ve made ___ friends in my new office.
We didn't get some rain this year.
ex.fixed: We didn't get any rain this year.

ex.q: How much times have you been to Mumbai?
ex.fixed: How many times have you been to Mumbai?

ex.q: There were less people than last year.
ex.fixed: There were fewer people than last year.
ex.y: With countable nouns, careful English uses “fewer”.

ex.a: I don't have any plans for Sunday.

ex.q: Correct this: “There are too much people here.”
a: There are too many people here

talk: Describe your kitchen or your office desk: what you have a lot of, what you have only a few of, and what you don’t have any of.
